Stated Claim / Post Context:
The plug-in balcony tech that could end high apartment power bills

Apartment dwellers need solar options.

Actual Article Body:

High-density living now defines much of Canberra and tens of thousands of renters and apartment owners are missing out on the renewable energy transition.

Login or signup to continue reading

As it stands, householders can slash their power bills using rooftop solar and batteries, apartment dwellers cannot. The territory's ban on plug-in solar technology leaves expensive rooftop installations and endless negotiations with owners corporations the only options.

This degree of difficulty means most unit dwellers settle for paying higher electricity prices. Solar is just too much trouble.

Plug-in solar could offer a fast, affordable fix with technology that is battle tested. More than one million plug-in solar systems already power homes and apartments across Germany. Renters simply buy the panels, attach them to a balcony, and plug them into a standard wall socket. Spain, New Zealand and Britain also use this technology.

The Canberra Liberals have urged territory and federal governments to legalise the devices, proposing a rollout by July next year, with existing rebates covering the equipment.

Environment spokeswoman Elizabeth Lee has championed the policy, noting it costs taxpayers absolutely nothing. She argues the program would deliver direct financial relief to the growing number of apartment residents.

Senate candidate Nick Tyrrell is another advocate who has highlighted the absurdity of delays. He argues Canberrans should not wait years for committee approvals when Germans can buy these "plug and play systems" off the shelf. Almost one-third of local homes are rented and these residents deserve a better deal.

Support extends across political divides. Federal Energy Minister Chris Bowen welcomes state and territory cooperation. He wants renters and apartment residents to access plug-in solar and battery systems. Western Australia leads the nation, announcing plans to legalise the technology. National energy ministers recently agreed to explore safe deployment pathways and will work with safety regulators to review equipment standards and strata laws.
